I saw a post in this subvoat that was just horribly wrong and decided that my response might be worthy of a submission by itself. (Edit: To the author of the other posts' credit, he contacted me and stated that he was not advocating refusing a field sobriety test, although that is how it sounded to me and several others.)

Having gotten a DUI, I took the time to really dive in and learn a lot about it. Below is practical stuff I learned and what to expect. If I can prevent anyone else from making my mistake then this post is worth it. I'll try and keep it to the point.

Drinking and Driving

Obvious stuff first:

  1. Don't do it.
  2. Plan ahead: timing. If you plan to leave at 1am, stop drinking at 11pm.
  3. Plan ahead: rides. Catch a ride to/from where you are going. Uber/Lyft are cheap options.
  4. Plan ahead: Buy a breathalyzer and know how to use it. You should wait 20 minutes after your last drink before testing, otherwise the residual alcohol in your mouth can give a false reading. Also, know where you are on the BAC vs time graph (see below). Just because you are legal to drive now, doesn't mean you will be in 30 minutes.
  5. Research: Some cities have volunteer programs to help you. In Utah, there is a program where you can call a number and two volunteers will show up. One will give you a ride, while the other will drive your car.

Maybe not so obvious stuff:

  1. Don't sleep it off in your car, at least, not in the driver's seat. In many states, this is enough to prove intent to drive and you can still get nailed for a DUI. Check your local laws. If you decide to sleep it off in your car, hide your keys (trunk, back seat, etc.) so they are not on your person. Again: don't sleep in the driver's seat.
  2. When you get your license from the DLD, you sign a contract. In this contract you agree to submit to a field sobriety test upon suspicion of driving under the influence. Refusal to submit to a test violates this contract and becomes a civil matter. (This is where the other posts' advice was just dead wrong). The act of simply refusing a test (even if you are sober) can result in you losing your license for 18+ months and result in arrest. (A DUI is a criminal matter and you'll go to court. The civil matter results in having to work with the DLD for breaking your contract).
  3. You can get a DUI for things not related to alcohol. Be careful of driving while taking any medication that makes you sleepy/not alert. This includes marijuana.
  4. Not talking to the police is a good rule of thumb. There are plenty of great YouTube videos about this subject. Also, know your local laws. In Utah, by law, you are required to give an officer your name and address.
  5. In Utah (check your laws), you can get a DUI on any vehicle: Car, skiing, hoverboard, skateboard, roller-blades, bicycle, a horse, electric wheelchair, etc. (This happened: A guy blacked-out in his electric wheelchair on an off-ramp off I15. He got a DUI. This also happened: Cops setup a checkpoint at the bottom of a ski slope and administered sobriety tests to snowboarders.)

Understand How Your Body Metabolizes Alcohol

  1. Body weight is a huge factor. Someone who is 90 lbs will get drunk a LOT faster than someone weighing 300 lbs. Going shot for shot with friends? Be careful.
  2. Myth: eating food will reduce your BAC. This isn't true. It may slow down the rate at which you metabolize alcohol, but in the end, the net sum of alcohol metabolized remains the same.
  3. At the time you use a breathalyzer, make sure your BAC is going down, not up. Understand the BAC vs time graph. Example. As you can see from the graph, about 45 minutes to an hour from your last drink and your BAC is on the decline. This will change if you are eating food / drinking a lot over time.
  4. If you need to speed-up reducing your BAC, start chugging water. Lots of it. Wait 10 minutes after you pee and re-test. Still not where you want to be? Slam more water, wait 10, pee, test, repeat.

Misc stuff

  1. In Utah, bar tenders / restaurants can be held liable if someone they served drives drunk. The fines are steep, and they can face jail time and can lose their liquor license.

I know I'll think of more stuff later. This is the basics of it. Feel free to hit me up with any questions about my experience, etc.

Construction Tips

Air flow is paramount, and from your description it's possibly being inhibited (hence the following points):

  1. Ensure there are enough holes in the grill, and ensure they're large enough.

  2. Ensure the small interleaved holes (around the base of the firebox) are above the top of the grill.

  3. Ensure the annular air gap between the fire box and outer body approximates the size of that shown in the video.

  4. Ensure the stove is as tall as the one in the video.

Operating Tips

  1. Ensure the wood used is dry.

  2. At 4800ft, try different woods (the pine should be good, but this suggestion is more of an experiment to gather more data).
